query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin nickel (Ni) wetting layer via physical vapor deposition (PVD) on tungsten (W) particles before copper (Cu) infiltration will enhance interfacial bonding and reduce void formation in W–Cu composites, thereby improving thermal transport and mechanical durability relative to conventional spark-plasma sintering or mechanical alloying methods.
generation.material_initial_state: W particles with native oxide layers and poor wettability embedded in a Cu matrix, which tends to exhibit phase separation, voids, and inhomogeneous thermal transport.
generation.intervention: Deposit a controlled, thin Ni coating on the W particles using physical vapor deposition (PVD) prior to low-temperature sintering in a vacuum or inert atmosphere.
generation.conditions: Processing at temperatures below the boiling point of Cu (to avoid Cu vaporization) and under vacuum/inert conditions; service conditions simulating irradiation environments in fusion-reactor joints.
generation.structural_mediator: The Ni coating improves the W–Cu interfacial contact by acting as a wetting layer that minimizes the formation of voids and phase segregation during sintering.
generation.mechanism: The Ni interlayer enhances wettability between W and Cu during sintering, leading to a more uniform and defect-free interface, which in turn reduces voids and improves thermal and mechanical connectivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Ni-coated W–Cu composite will exhibit improved thermal conductivity and enhanced mechanical durability (e.g., higher fracture strength and reduced defect density) compared to composites produced without the Ni coating.
generation.baseline: Conventional fabrication methods such as spark-plasma sintering or mechanical alloying without the application of a pre-coating, which typically result in phase separation, void formation, and compromised thermal performance.
generation.boundary: The intervention is effective when processing is conducted below Cu’s boiling point under vacuum/inert conditions and the material is used under service-like irradiation conditions typical of fusion-reactor joints.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvements in thermal transport and mechanical properties are uncertain, and the long-term stability of the Ni wetting layer under irradiation has not been fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of W–Cu composites: one set with a PVD-applied thin Ni coating on W particles and a control set without the coating. Both sets will undergo identical low-temperature sintering in a vacuum. After processing, subject the samples to thermal cycling and irradiation to simulate fusion-reactor conditions.
measurements: High-resolution microscopy (e.g., SEM/TEM) to quantify void content and inspect interfacial quality
Thermal conductivity measurements using laser flash analysis
Mechanical tests including fracture toughness and compressive strength both before and after simulated irradiation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the Ni-coated samples do not show a statistically significant (e.g., ≥20% improvement) reduction in interfacial voids and enhancement in thermal/mechanical properties compared to the control samples, or if no improvement is observed after irradiation testing.

chosen.lever: interfacial chemistry via wetting layer modification
chosen.technique: physical vapor deposition (PVD) to apply a thin Ni coating on W particles, followed by controlled low‐temperature sintering
chosen.conditions: processing below Cu boiling temperature in a vacuum or inert atmosphere and service conditions simulating irradiation in fusion-reactor joints
chosen.why: This intervention directly addresses the performance-limiting phase separation and void formation by engineering the W–Cu interface to improve wettability and bonding. It builds upon prior evidence from vapor-coated powders achieving near-perfect contact, and it is a standard approach in materials science that preserves mechanical durability while enhancing thermal transport. The method can be implemented with routine PVD and sintering equipment, making it the most plausible single intervention that overcomes existing fabrication limitations.
